newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr keeps nerve on US$, flees from yen.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr keeps nerve on US$, flees from yen.

text.p: The Australian dollar spent much of Thursday submerged beneath a wave of offshore selling, but did get a late lifeline on domestic rates which at least kept it afloat against the U.S. dollar.

It took an early hammering on the crosses as Japanese investors bailed out of long dollar positions and came close to breaching month-old US$0.7720 support as rumours circulated the Reserve Bank board would meet especially to discuss a rate cut.
But it bounced when RBA governor Ian Macfarlane said recent wages data had been a setback to prospects for low inflation and the bank would not run the economy faster than was safe.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the dollar was holding its own at US$0.7762/67 after delving as deep as US$0.7724 ahead of Macfarlane's speech.

The finish was still down on Wednesday's late US$0.7782/87 but within the US$0.7720/7860 range held for more than a month. A break of the floor would have been a technical disaster and seen it to US$0.7680 enroute to US$0.7620 and points beyond.

Traders said the selling had been led, once again, by a local-based U.S. bank which was joined by heavy Japanese sales of AUD/yen when US$/yen tumbled. The U.S. bank was also seen buying bill futures, which helped fuel the rate cut talk.
Bids from exporters and a well-known Chinese name helped arrest the slide and Macfarlane's warning on wages forced further short covering.
Indeed, many dealers were non-plussed by the sudden revival of easing rumours given Macfarlane only last week said there was no economic benefit in a policy move now.

Most analysts had concluded that since recent wages data implied a threat to inflation the RBA would not risk another cut. The latest figures on average weekly ordinary time earnings showed stronger than expected growth of 1.3 percent in the three months to February.
That took annual wages growth to 4.6 percent from 3.9 percent the quarter before and into the 4.5-5.0 percent zone which the RBA has expressed concerns about in the past.

Some, however, felt the wages danger was exaggerated and the breakdown of private and public sector AWOTE, to be released on May 22, would support their argument by showing growth had been biased upwards by special circumstances in the public sector.

They figured that if private sector growth -- which is more indicative of demand and supply pressures in the economy -- was well below the aggregate level, as they expected, then the RBA could still have scope for a rate cut.

Traders said this argument must have some adherents in the market since the June 90-day bank bill contract was actually five basis points higher after the speech at 94.05, implying a rate of 5.95 percent against the present official 6.00 percent.

The dollar's troubles on the crosses were international in origin as a collapse in US$/yen spooked Japanese investors into cutting unhedged A$ bond positions as well as carry trades -- where investors borrow in yen at low rates and lend in A$ at much higher yields.
The currency dived as a result to 90.13/23 yen from 92.57/67 late here Wednesday and a 100.03 peak just a fortnight ago.
The selling took its toll on the trade weighted index which skidded to 58.8 from 59.5 late Wednesday.
In this it has mirrored the U.S. dollar which has dived to 116.17/27 from a 127.46 yen high.
The reversal partly refected fears the Japanese authorities had been preparing to intervene to end the yen's slide and were also considering raising interest rates from their record lows.

The U.S. dollar's decline was fuelled overnight when a soft producer price report encouraged speculation the Federal Reserve might not hike rates at its policy meeting next week and rumours circulated the Treasury wanted to see US$/yen at 115.00 yen.
There was no confirmation from the Treasury, and dealers felt it highly unlikely given Treasury Secretary Rubin's oft-stated desire to see a strong dollar.

But it did mesh with recent thinking in Japanese circles that MOF forex guru Sakakibara favoured 115.00 as the mid rate for US$/yen. Technical analysts said the break of key 117.50 support confirmed a trend reversal was underway and the next key chart target would be 109.25 with 103.00 even possible.
The matching targets for the local currency would be 84.35 yen and 79.50.
